sections.title: 1.1 Fundamental & Derived Quantities
sections.content:
In Physics, a physical quantity is any property of a body or system that can be measured with an instrument and expressed as a numerical value accompanied by a unit. In Nigeria, whether you are buying 5kg of semovita at the market or checking the speed of a Danfo bus on the Third Mainland Bridge, you are dealing with physical quantities! Fundamental quantities (also called base quantities) are basic physical quantities that do not depend on any other physical quantity for their definition. They serve as the foundation for all other measurements in science. There are seven (7) fundamental physical quantities in the SI system. They include:
Length: Metre (m)
Mass: Kilogram (kg)
Time: Second (s)
Electric Current: Ampere (A)
Temperature: Kelvin (K)
Amount of Substance: Mole (mol)
Luminous Intensity: Candela (cd)
Fundamental quantities cannot be broken down into simpler physical quantities. Mass vs Weight: Mass is a fundamental quantity measured in $\text{kg}$. Weight is a derived quantity (force) measured in Newtons ($\text{N}$). Derived Physical Quantities and Their Units. Derived quantities are physical quantities obtained by combining two or more fundamental quantities through mathematical operations like multiplication or division. Common examples of derived physical quantities include: $\mathbf{Area}$: Obtained by multiplying length by length ($\text{Length} \times \text{Length}$). Unit is $\text{m}^2$.
$\mathbf{Volume}$: Obtained by multiplying three length dimensions ($\text{Length} \times \text{Length} \times \text{Length}$). Unit is $\text{m}^3$.
$\mathbf{Density}$: This is obtained by dividing mass by volume ($\text{Mass} / \text{Volume}$). Unit is $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}$.
$\mathbf{Speed/Velocity}$: Obtained by dividing distance or displacement by time ($\text{Length} / \text{Time}$). Unit is $\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$.
Derivation of Units from Fundamental Quantities
To derive the SI unit of any physical quantity: Write down the defining mathematical formula for the quantity. Substitute the S.I base unit for each fundamental quantity in the formula. Simplify the expression using laws of indices. Example 1: Deriving the S.I Unit of Force $$\text{Force} = \text{Mass} \times \text{Acceleration}$$ $$\text{F} = \text{ma}$$ Unit of Mass $= \text{kg}$ Unit of Acceleration = $\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ Derived Unit of Force $= \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ or Newton (N).
Example 2: Deriving the SI Unit of Pressure $$\text{Pressure} = \frac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}}$$
But Unit of Force = $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ Unit of Area = $\text{m}^2$
There derived Unit of Pressure $= \frac{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^2} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ (commonly called the Pascal, symbol $\text{Pa}$).
JAMB Exam Focus:JAMB frequently asks candidates to identify which quantity in a given list is fundamental or derived.
Remember that Mass is measured in $\text{kg}$ (not grams), and Temperature is measured in $\text{K}$ (not Celsius). Expect questions asking for the base SI unit equivalent of derived units like Newtons ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$), Joules ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$), or Watts ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-3}$).

sections.title: Measurement of Length, Area, and Volume
sections.content:
Length is defined as the distance between two distinct points in space. The choice of instrument depends on the magnitude of the length and the degree of accuracy required. 1. Metre Rule: - Measuring Range: $1\text{ cm}$ to $100\text{ cm}$ ($1\text{ m}$). - Least Count / Accuracy: $0.1\text{ cm}$ or $1\text{ mm}$. Application: - Measuring room dimensions, cloth at Balogun market, or laboratory benches. Major Error: Parallax Error — caused by reading the scale with eyes positioned obliquely rather than perpendicularly directly above the mark. 2. Vernier Calipers: - Measuring Range: $1\text{ cm}$ to $15\text{ cm}$. - Least Count / Accuracy: $0.01\text{ cm}$ or $0.1\text{ mm}$. Features: - Inside jaws (for internal diameters), outside jaws (for external diameters), and depth stem (for beaker depths). - Reading Formula: $$\text{Total Reading} = \text{Main Scale Reading (MSR)} + (\text{Vernier Scale Reading (VSR)} \times \text{Least Count})$$ 3. Micrometer Screw Gauge: - Measuring Range: $0\text{ cm}$ to $2.5\text{ cm}$. - Least Count / Accuracy: $0.001\text{ cm}$ or $0.01\text{ mm}$ (Most precise!). Features: - Anvil, spindle, sleeve scale (main scale), thimble scale (circular scale), and ratchet (prevents over-tightening). Application: - Measuring wire thickness, sheet metal gauge, or razor blade thickness. Reading Formula: $$\text{Total Reading} = \text{Sleeve Reading} + (\text{Thimble Reading} \times 0.01\text{ mm})$$ $\underline{\text{Measurement of Area and Volume}}$ Regular Solid Area and Volume: Determined using standard mathematical formulas. - Area of rectangle $= l \times b$ - Volume of cylinder $= \pi r^2 h$ - Volume of sphere $= \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ Irregular Solid Volume: Determined using a Measuring Cylinder or Eureka Can via the Displacement Method. 1. Fill the measuring cylinder with water to an initial volume $V_1$. 2. Gently submerge the irregular solid (e.g., a small stone) completely using a thread. 3. Record the new final water volume $V_2$. $$\text{Volume of Irregular Solid} = V_2 - V_1$$
JAMB Exam Focus: JAMB often presents scale diagrams of Vernier Calipers or Micrometer Screw Gauges and asks candidates to calculate the exact reading. Questions on parallax error and meniscus reading precautions are extremely common in both UTME and WAEC practical objectives.

sections.title: 1.3 Measurement of Mass and Time
sections.content:
Mass is defined as the quantity of matter contained within a physical body.
SI Unit: Kilogram ($\text{kg}$). 
Sub-units: Gram ($\text{g}$), Milligram ($\text{mg}$), Tonne ($\text{t}$).
$1\text{ kg} = 1,000\text{ g}$$1\text{ tonne} = 1,000\text{ kg}$

Property: Mass is an intrinsic scalar property; it remains constant regardless of location (Earth, Moon, or deep space).
